claims.claim: News is working defined as reports of recent, significant events; journalism is the activity of gathering, assessing, creating, and presenting news and information, and the product of those activities.

Journalism's distinctive purpose is to provide people with verified information they can use to make better decisions, which is what separates it from talk, entertainment, opinion, advertising, and propaganda.

Conventional news values include timeliness (newness), significance or impact, proximity (closeness), conflict, and human interest; journalism training manuals frame the core tests as whether an event is new, unusual, interesting or significant, and about people, with closeness and personal impact as story-strengthening factors.

News organizations distinguish news reports from opinion content: op-eds and bylined commentary are labeled and separated from straight reporting, and professional codes require labeling advocacy and commentary.
The purpose of news is to inform; presenting non-news as news merely because it entertains violates the news-versus-entertainment distinction.

The norm of objectivity took shape in the early twentieth century, especially the 1920s: after the nineteenth-century realism idea that arranging facts would reveal truth, critics such as Walter Lippmann and Charles Merz (1919) argued that journalists needed a common method of testing information, and the original concept was that the method, not the journalist, is objective.

Objectivity is a contested norm: critics argue that reporting always occurs through a lens of personal experience, culture, and background; that a neutral voice without verification can create a veneer over unverified or one-sided reporting; and that empirical studies (such as the contested 2005 Groseclose and Milyo analysis) find measurable slant in U.S. news outlets.

The news production process runs from reporting and sourcing through verification and editing: reporters gather information through observation, interviews, and documents; sources are identified (with anonymity reserved for those who might face harm); editors work with reporters to verify sources and double-check facts; and the inverted pyramid places the most important facts first.

Fact-checking and corrections are professional norms: codes require verifying information before release and acknowledging mistakes and correcting them promptly and prominently, and newsrooms publish corrections and, in notable cases, apologies; fabrication is treated as a career-ending violation (Jayson Blair at the New York Times, 2003; Stephen Glass at The New Republic, 1998).

Journalism ethics are organized around accuracy, fairness, independence, and accountability: the SPJ Code of Ethics names four principles (Seek Truth and Report It; Minimize Harm; Act Independently; Be Accountable and Transparent), and the vital information premise holds that news media exist to give citizens the accurate and reliable information they need to function in a democracy, including a watchdog role over government and business.

The news ecosystem combines local and national outlets, wire services, and round-the-clock digital distribution: local papers often practice consensus-style journalism serving their communities; the Associated Press was founded in 1846 as a cooperative of five New York papers sharing telegraph-delivered news; radio carried first live breaking-news coverage in 1916; the 1963 Kennedy assassination is widely described as the beginning of round-the-clock television news; and the internet has made instant digital distribution and news aggregation the norm, sharpening the tension between being first and being right.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What does objectivity mean, and can it be achieved?
positions: Objectivity is impartiality: reporters can and should write without bias, the stance associated with the late-nineteenth-century turn to neutral reporting exemplified by the 1896 New York Times.

Objectivity is a method, not a state: journalists are always subject to bias, and what is objective is a consistent discipline of verification (Lippmann; Kovach and Rosenstiel as summarized by the American Press Institute).

Objectivity as commonly understood is unattainable: reporting always passes through personal and cultural lenses, and a neutral-sounding voice can mask bias (University of Minnesota open textbook; contested bias research such as Groseclose and Milyo 2005).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents objectivity as a contested professional norm with an attributed history and named critiques; it does not declare any position settled.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do all news reports contain bias?
positions: The University of Minnesota open textbook states that all news stories contain some bias because of the diversity of journalists' perspectives.
Strict defenders of objectivity hold that bias is a failure that method and discipline can and should eliminate from reporting.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an open debate; the lesson says ethical practice aims at fairness, verification, and completeness rather than claiming a bias-free state.

sourceRecords.title: What is journalism? Definition and meaning of the craft
sourceRecords.notes: The live URL now returns 404 after an API site restructure; read the Wayback Machine capture of 2021-01-25 (web.archive.org/web/20210125204700/https://www.americanpressinstitute.org/journalism-essentials/what-is-journalism/). Supports: journalism as the activity of gathering, assessing, creating, and presenting news and information, and the product of those activities; and, via the companion page in the same capture ('What makes journalism different than other forms of communication?'), journalism's purpose of providing people with verified information they can use to make better decisions, which distinguishes it from talk, entertainment, opinion, assertion, advertising, and propaganda. Content based on the Committee of Concerned Journalists' research (author Walter Dean; Tom Rosenstiel formerly co-chaired the committee). Facts only; prose fully synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: The lost meaning of 'objectivity'
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the Wayback Machine capture of 2021-01-25 because the live URL returns 404 after the API site restructure. Based on Bill Kovach and Tom Rosenstiel's The Elements of Journalism and the Committee of Concerned Journalists. Supports: the 1920s emergence of objectivity as a professional norm responding to the recognition that journalists are biased, calling for a consistent method of testing information; the earlier nineteenth-century 'realism' idea that arranging facts reveals truth; the 1919 Lippmann and Merz critique of New York Times coverage of the Russian Revolution; the formulation 'the method is objective, not the journalist'; and the critique that a neutral voice without a discipline of verification can create a veneer over unverified or one-sided reporting. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: SPJ Code of Ethics
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the Wayback Machine capture of 2024-06-01 (web.archive.org/web/20240601000000/https://www.spj.org/ethicscode.asp) because the live URL currently returns 404 while SPJ publishes a proposed-revision notice on spj.org. Code revised September 6, 2014. Supports the four principles (Seek Truth and Report It; Minimize Harm; Act Independently; Be Accountable and Transparent) and the provisions to verify information before releasing it, that neither speed nor format excuses inaccuracy, to gather, update, and correct information throughout the life of a story, to identify sources and reserve anonymity for those who might face harm, to label advocacy and commentary, to avoid and disclose conflicts of interest, and to acknowledge mistakes and correct them promptly and prominently. Reference only; no code wording reproduced verbatim beyond the principle names. URL updated 2026-08-21 to the live canonical page; originally read via a 2024-06-01 Wayback capture of the former URL.
